concepts.name: Grand Trunk Road: Origins, Extent, and Historical Nomenclature
key_dimensions: Pre-Sher Shah existence as 'Uttarapatha' and its Mauryan-era antecedents — trap: Sher Shah built it vs. renovated it
Terminal points: Sonargaon (Bengal) to Peshawar/Attock — exact endpoints frequently tested
Multiple historical names: Sadak-e-Azam, Badshahi Sadak, Shah Rah-e-Azam — UPSC tests which name belongs to which era
Comparison with Mauryan Royal Highway described by Megasthenes — overlap and distinction

concepts.name: Total Road Network: Scale, Coverage, and the Four Principal Highways
key_dimensions: Four major roads: Agra to Burhanpur, Agra to Jodhpur/Chittor, Agra to Mandu, Lahore to Multan — exact routes tested
Total length estimates (~1500 kos or ~4000 miles) — distinguishing total network from GT Road alone
Strategic vs. commercial rationale: military mobility vs. trade facilitation debate
Comparison with Akbar's road network — trap of attributing later Mughal improvements to Sher Shah

concepts.name: Sarai (Caravanserai) System: Structure, Spacing, and Administrative Function
key_dimensions: Number of sarais: ~1700 sarais built — distinguishing from later Mughal additions
Spacing interval: approximately every 2 kos (~8 km) — frequently tested measurement
Dual function: rest houses for travelers AND intelligence/postal relay stations — often only one function cited in options
Separate quarters for Hindus and Muslims within sarais — social inclusivity dimension

concepts.name: Postal (Dak) System: Mechanism and Integration with Road Infrastructure
key_dimensions: Horse relay system using sarais as postal stations — distinguishing from foot messenger systems
Administrative intelligence function: sarais doubled as information-gathering nodes for the state
Comparison with Mauryan postal system and later Mughal adaptations — continuity vs. innovation trap
Role of the system in rapid troop mobilization and revenue administration

concepts.name: Shade Trees Along Roads: Species, Purpose, and Symbolic Significance
key_dimensions: Planting of shady trees (mango, banyan) along roadsides — welfare dimension of infrastructure
Distance markers (kos minars) planted alongside trees — combined infrastructure package
Abbas Khan Sarwani's 'Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi' as primary source for this detail — source-based question trap
Comparison with Ashoka's tree-planting edicts — UPSC loves cross-period comparisons

concepts.name: Kos Minars (Milestone Pillars): Design, Spacing, and Administrative Purpose
key_dimensions: Placed every 2 kos (~6-8 km) — distinguishing kos minar spacing from sarai spacing (both ~2 kos but different sources give variations)
Function: distance measurement, waymarker for travelers, administrative surveying tool
Survival of kos minars as archaeological evidence — UNESCO/ASI protected structures
Akbar's continuation and expansion of kos minar system — attribution trap between Sher Shah and Akbar

concepts.name: Wells and Water Provision Along Highways
key_dimensions: Construction of wells at regular intervals as welfare infrastructure
Integration of wells within sarai compounds vs. standalone roadside wells — distinction matters
Reflects the 'welfare state' dimension of Sher Shah's administration — frequently linked to his overall governance philosophy
Comparison with Firuz Shah Tughlaq's canal/well construction — overlap trap in welfare infrastructure

concepts.name: Mosques Within Sarais: Religious Infrastructure and State Patronage
key_dimensions: Each sarai reportedly contained a mosque — religious dimension of a secular infrastructure project
Reflects syncretic vs. Islamic governance debate about Sher Shah's administration
Distinction between state-built mosques and traveler-donation mosques within sarais
UPSC trap: using mosque-in-sarai as evidence of religious discrimination vs. standard Sultanate-era practice

concepts.name: Administrative Officials (Shiqqdars) Assigned to Sarais: Security and Maintenance
key_dimensions: Appointment of shiqqdars and chaukidars for road/sarai security — distinguishing roles
Village headmen (muqaddams) held responsible for crimes on road segments — collective responsibility system
Integration of road security with broader law-and-order administration
Comparison with Alauddin Khalji's market regulation officials — administrative overlap trap

concepts.name: Road Infrastructure and Revenue/Trade Facilitation: The Customs and Toll Connection
key_dimensions: Sher Shah rationalized customs duties alongside road building — infrastructure-revenue nexus
Reduction of internal toll points to only three: Bengal, the Punjab, and the Indus crossing
Roads enabled standardized weight/measure enforcement and currency circulation
UPSC trap: conflating road-building with complete elimination of tolls (he reduced, not eliminated)

concepts.name: Military-Strategic Dimension of Road Network
key_dimensions: Roads designed for rapid troop deployment — GT Road's strategic value from Bengal to NWFP
Sarai system as military logistics chain — grain and fodder storage for armies
Road network's role in Sher Shah's rapid conquest of Humayun — connecting infrastructure to military success
Later Mughal and British use of the same road network — legacy and continuity angle

concepts.name: Sources and Historiography: Abbas Khan Sarwani and Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi
key_dimensions: 'Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi' as the principal Persian source for Sher Shah's infrastructure — written during Akbar's reign (posthumous account trap)
Potential hagiographic bias in Sarwani's account — source criticism dimension
Other sources: Baburnama references to pre-existing roads, European traveler accounts of GT Road
UPSC source-identification questions: which text describes the sarai system?

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Infrastructure vs. Mughal Continuity: Attribution Controversies
key_dimensions: Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan all added to GT Road and sarai network — correct attribution critical
British colonial documentation of GT Road often credits Sher Shah — but also notes Mughal additions
Rudyard Kipling's 'Kim' reference to GT Road — cultural legacy angle sometimes used in UPSC mains
Trap question: which ruler built the maximum number of sarais? (Often Akbar, not Sher Shah)

concepts.name: Infrastructure as Welfare Administration: Sher Shah's Governance Philosophy
key_dimensions: Roads, sarais, wells, and trees as integrated welfare package — not isolated construction projects
Sher Shah's own statement (per Sarwani): 'I have conquered kingdoms... but the sarais are my greatest achievement' — direct quote trap
Welfare infrastructure compared to Ashoka's edicts on road amenities — standard UPSC comparison
Distinction between revenue-motivated infrastructure and welfare-motivated infrastructure in historiographical debate

concepts.name: Bengal to Sind Road Connectivity: Economic and Political Integration
key_dimensions: GT Road as instrument of political unification of the subcontinent's north — not merely a trade route
Connection to Sher Shah's administrative centralization: fast communication = tighter control
Impact on Bengal's integration with the Delhi-centered political economy
Comparison with Mauryan integration of peripheral regions through road networks

concepts.name: Road Infrastructure and Standardized Currency Circulation
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's rupiya (silver) and dam (copper) coins circulated efficiently due to road network
Roads enabled price equalization across regions — economic integration argument
Sarai system as nodes for currency exchange and commercial dispute resolution
UPSC trap: attributing rupee standardization solely to road infrastructure vs. monetary reform itself

concepts.name: Comparison of Sher Shah's Road Network with Pre-existing Sultanate Infrastructure
key_dimensions: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's canal network vs. Sher Shah's road network — different infrastructure priorities
Alauddin Khalji's market towns on roads vs. Sher Shah's sarai system — functional overlap
Whether Sher Shah's roads were original construction or renovation of existing tracks — historiographical debate
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's failed administrative transfers (reliance on poor roads) — contrast with Sher Shah's solution

concepts.name: British Colonial Use and Documentation of the Grand Trunk Road
key_dimensions: British renamed/extended GT Road as part of colonial communication network — continuity trap
Lord Dalhousie's railway alignment often followed GT Road — infrastructure legacy
Colonial-era surveys documenting Sher Shah's original mile markers — archaeological validation
UPSC mains angle: colonial infrastructure building on Sher Shah's template as example of path dependency
